Prevention: Prevention particulaly important as difficult to contol.
Seeds considered unimportant;tubers are the main means of spread
Clean tools and farm machinery to prevent tubers being spread
Do not accept potentially contaminated materials, e.g. soil on planting stock
Control established populations near waterways to prevent spread during flooding and storm events
Promote cover crops such as legume crops like alfalfa to suppress establishment
Monitoring: Erect, perennial sedge (30-60 cm high), with extensive underground network of tubers.
Tubers dark brown/black, irregular shaped, 1-2 cm long at maturity, with several buds.
Leaves linear with distinct midrib, 7 mm wide.
Inflorescence with several unequal 'branches', each 2-6 cm long, emerging from the tip of the stem; each with 3-8 purplish-brown flowerheads.
Regularly inspect fields, at least fortnightly and in particular during and shortly after the wet season, and consider direct control when found
Look our for it in low spots, wetlands and along waterways.
Water and storm events can spread tubers
Regular monitoring at least fortinightly at beginning of every growing season. (over 10 sedge plants /m2 control with glyphosate)
Direct Control (Non-chemical): Tubers and rhizomes in the soil can be destroyed by dessication (most effective in dry soil) or exhausting food reserves.
Cultivate every 2-3 weeks until crop canopy forms: the weed is shade intolerant
Place organic mulch over areas where the weed is expect to grow: provides temporary suppression
Black polyethylene sheet can be used in high value crops as a barrier or for soil solarization
Tillage must be deep (>12cm) in order to disturb as many of the rhizomes and tubers as possible.
Do this under dry conditions so the exposed rhizomes dessicate.
Fortnightly spot weeding should be carried out
Planting: before planting seed, allow the weed to emerge after the rains/ irrigation for early control with post emergence herbicide
Bromacil at recommended rate (2 lt/ha) to be used to suppress the weed until crop canopy develops to suppress the weed.
Direct Control (Chemical): Use of chemical herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage
Most effective herbicide is glyhposate, applied post-emergence at the flowering stage, at 3L/ ha (480g a.e.
Repeated applications when you see the weed within a season, to eliminate weed in an area, at 2L/ha (480g a.e.
Restrictions: U (unlikely to present acute hazard in normal use)
